title: He Scored an Unbeaten 75 in the Final. Two Weeks Later, the Scan Showed a Tear Nobody Expected.
excerpt: Virat Kohli's rare distal semimembranosus tendon tear rules him out of India's first-ever bilateral ODI series against Afghanistan — but England in July remains the target
body:
When Virat Kohli walked off the Narendra Modi Stadium on the night of May 31, he had just guided Royal Challengers Bengaluru to a second consecutive IPL title. His unbeaten 75 — composed, urgent, built around the kind of risk-calibration that only a man with 14,797 ODI runs has — anchored a five-wicket victory over Gujarat Titans in Ahmedabad.

He looked, by the end of it, slightly uncomfortable. Nothing dramatic. A tightness in the back of his left leg, a minor adjustment in his gait between the boundary and the dressing room. Two weeks and one MRI later, the picture is considerably less reassuring.

Kohli has been diagnosed with a **distal semimembranosus tendon tear** — a rare variant of hamstring injury that affects the tendon near the back of the knee rather than the more common tears higher up the thigh. It is unusual enough that even the BCCI medical staff did not initially suspect it. Scans confirmed what the discomfort had hinted at, and India's selection committee had no choice but to rule him out of the three-match ODI series against Afghanistan, starting Saturday in Dharamsala.

"With Virat at this point, it's just been less than a week since he injured himself in the finals. We don't know the timelines yet," chief selector Ajit Agarkar said. "But it looks like he might be fit for that England one-day series. It's not a definitive answer, so don't hold me to it."

The timing is particularly frustrating. Since retiring from both Tests and T20 Internationals, Kohli has committed himself exclusively to ODI cricket. Every series now matters — not as a warm-up for another format, but as the format itself. India play 20 ODIs before the 2027 World Cup in South Africa, and each one is a brick in whatever team they are trying to build.

Kohli's absence from Dharamsala means Yashasvi Jaiswal, who replaced him in the squad, may get an opportunity at number three — a position the 24-year-old left-hander has rarely occupied in international cricket. Ishan Kishan, recalled to the ODI setup after nearly three years away, is another candidate. Either way, someone will bat in the spot that Kohli has made his own for the better part of a decade.

## The Recovery and the Road Ahead

Fresh reports suggest the injury is not as severe as the diagnosis initially implied. Kohli is responding well to treatment and is expected to be available for India's three-match ODI series in England, starting July 14 at Edgbaston in Birmingham.

For NRIs in the United Kingdom, that is meaningful news. Kohli — who has been based in London for the past few years — is deeply familiar with English conditions. His career record in England across formats is formidable: 54 ODI centuries, 14,797 runs at an average of 58.72, and the kind of presence that fills stadiums. A fit Kohli arriving in Birmingham, Cardiff, and Lord's in mid-July would not only strengthen India's batting but give the Indian diaspora in Britain a reason to pack those stands.

## The Broader Concern

Beyond the specifics of this injury, Kohli's absence also highlights the increasingly delicate balance India must manage with their senior players. Rohit Sharma, 39, has been cleared to play in Dharamsala after his own IPL-related hamstring scare. Hardik Pandya, who was initially included in the squad, has been ruled out with a new quadriceps strain suffered during his fitness test at the Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru — an injury that happened, remarkably, while he was being tested to prove he was injury-free.

India's 2027 World Cup squad, when it crystallizes, will almost certainly include Kohli. But the margin for these bodies is getting thinner. The question is no longer whether Kohli can perform — 675 runs in 16 IPL matches, including that unbeaten 75 in the final, settled that question comprehensively — but whether the system around him can keep him on the field long enough to matter when it counts.

For now, the only certain thing is this: on Saturday afternoon in Dharamsala, when Shubman Gill leads India out for the first ODI of a historic bilateral series against Afghanistan, Virat Kohli will be watching from London.
